strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem with a straightforward adaptation of Mixup to autoregressive instruction tuning. The confidence partitioning, token-level interpolation, and combined training objective are clearly organized and require no additional annotations.

The empirical trend is consistently positive across two model families and three training datasets. Table 1 reports improvements in all four model–dataset combinations, including approximately 0.20–0.29 MT-Bench points and 0.32–1.67 percentage points in length-controlled AlpacaEval win rate. Medical QA accuracy improves by 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points on average for Llama and Mistral, respectively.
Human evaluation provides useful corroboration beyond automated judging: across 200 judgments on 80 instructions, SFTMix receives 42.5% preference versus 26.5% for NTP, with 31% ties.

Experiments with a smaller reference model, LoRA, and two data selection methods demonstrate useful compatibility. Ablations also examine the regularization weight, retention of the NTP objective, and which examples receive NTP supervision.
weaknesses: The central claim that confidence-based pairing is crucial lacks a decisive control. There is no comparison against random pairing or within-confidence pairing on the same dataset with the same objective and training budget. Section 5.2 instead introduces GPT-4 responses and tests quality-based pairing, without evaluating confidence-based pairing on that modified dataset. Consequently, the improvements cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed confidence partition. This is a principal obstacle to a clear Findings recommendation.

Evaluation uncertainty and model selection are insufficiently controlled. Appendix B.1 selects the regularization weight using MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2, the same benchmarks used for reporting the Llama/Alpaca results; no separate validation set is described. Repeated evaluation rounds do not establish robustness across training seeds, and no confidence intervals or paired significance tests accompany the sometimes small gains. Transfer to other settings is encouraging but does not resolve these issues.

The proposed mechanism is substantially stronger than the supporting evidence. A t-SNE visualization of extreme-confidence examples and a small task-type inspection do not demonstrate that confident examples overfit, that unconfident examples generalize poorly, or that SFTMix specifically remedies either behavior. Confidence also reflects response predictability and noise. Held-out performance or generalization-gap analyses by confidence group would be more diagnostic. Appendix A establishes a change in gradients, without establishing the claimed generalization effects.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite reporting several training hyperparameters. The manuscript lacks a code link, the reference-checkpoint collection schedule, prompt and truncation settings, loss-normalization details, LoRA configuration, and precise GPT-4 judge configuration. The human evaluation omits annotator counts, allocation of judgments, presentation randomization, and agreement. The cross-entropy sign convention is also inconsistent between Section 3 and Appendix A.

The practical cost is insufficiently characterized. SFTMix requires a separate reference fine-tuning run and scoring at multiple checkpoints, but total compute and memory overhead are not reported. The smaller-reference and LoRA experiments support feasibility; quantitative cost accounting is needed to substantiate the claims concerning compute-constrained use and scalability.

The broader methodological contribution needs clearer positioning against existing cartography-guided Mixup, particularly the cited Park and Caragea (2022), and relevant instruction-tuning regularizers such as NEFTune. Establishing the value of the autoregressive adaptation would strengthen the main-conference case. This contribution question is separate from the experimental controls and reproducibility concerns underlying the borderline Findings assessment.
